definition: Depravity means a state of deep moral corruption or wickedness in a person's underlying character.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word depravity. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know depravity should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The novelist reveals her villain's depravity slowly, one cold-blooded choice at a time, until readers grasp how rotten his character truly is.
Misconduct describes bad behavior in one setting — a broken rule, an abused position; depravity describes a character that is corrupt through and through.
Depravity names deep moral corruption inside a person; evil goes even further, suggesting active, deliberate malice toward others.

Wickedness is deep moral badness wherever it shows — a wicked act, a wicked scheme, a wicked heart. Depravity pushes the idea inward and downward: it names a character so thoroughly corrupt that the badness is the person's settled state, not a quality of this or that deed.

Immorality is the broad failure to follow moral principles, and it covers everything from cheating at cards to far worse. Depravity is immorality at the bottom of the scale and rooted in character — not a lapse or a bad patch but a nature corrupted through and through.

Degeneracy tells a story of decline: something or someone that was better has slid downward into corruption. Depravity needs no such fall — it names the corrupt state itself, however it arose. A degenerate court was once noble; a depraved one may never have been anything else.

Latin pravus meant 'crooked, wrong,' and de- pushes it all the way: twisted through and through. Critics called the dictator's final orders depraved — the acts of a character gone completely crooked.
Depravity means a state of deep moral corruption or wickedness in a person's underlying character.
In her lecture, the historian traced how court records portrayed the deposed king's depravity — his cruelty, his greed, and his utter indifference to his starving subjects.

The records describe the ruler's whole moral character as corrupt — a lasting inner state shown across many behaviors, not one isolated bad act — and that underlying corrupt quality is what depravity names.
Depravity is a noun for a person's underlying corrupt moral nature — a lasting state, not a single act.
Two adjectives taught in other lessons of this unit cover nearby ground: heinous describes how shockingly evil one particular act is, and nefarious describes a scheming, villainous person or plot.
Reserve depravity for the rotten character underneath: a single terrible act might reveal a lifetime of depravity.

When a notorious pirate captain finally faced trial, the testimony that shocked the court did not concern the stolen cargo at all.
Sailors described cruelties inflicted after ships had already surrendered, when nothing remained to be gained.
Greed, the judges knew, could explain almost anything a pirate did.
One prosecutor called it depravity: not a temper that flared and passed, but a corruption that seemed to sit at the very center of the man's character.
Even his own crew, hardened men with much to answer for, testified that his cruelty had been constant from the first day they knew him.
